name: Thomas Jefferson
info: Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826) was a Virginia planter and lawyer, the primary author of the Declaration of Independence and the third president of the United States from 1801 to 1809, and a lifelong slave owner.

facts.born: 13 April 1743 (2 April 1743, Old Style) at Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia; third of ten children of Peter Jefferson, a planter and surveyor, and Jane Randolph
facts.died: 4 July 1826 at 12:50 p.m., aged 83, on the 50th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration of Independence; buried at Monticello under an epitaph he wrote
facts.role: Member of Virginia's House of Burgesses (1769–1775); delegate to the Second Continental Congress (1775); governor of Virginia (1779–1781); Minister to France (1785–1789); first Secretary of State (1790–1793); vice president (1797–1801); third president of the United States (1801–1809); founder and first rector of the University of Virginia
facts.known: primary author of the Declaration of Independence; the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom; the Louisiana Purchase of 1803; the Lewis and Clark expedition; the founding of the University of Virginia; Monticello; ownership of about 600 enslaved people over his lifetime

t: Born into a slave-owning Virginia family, Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence in June 1776 and went on to serve as governor, minister to France, secretary of state, vice president and, from 1801 to 1809, president.

As president he doubled the size of the United States through the Louisiana Purchase, sent Lewis and Clark to the Pacific and reduced the national debt from $83 million to $57 million, but his Embargo Act of 1807 brought economic chaos.
He wrote that slavery was harmful to slave and master, yet he enslaved about 600 people over his lifetime, and scholars give sharply differing readings of his views and conduct.
dyk: Jefferson's first library, of about 200 volumes, was destroyed in a fire at Shadwell in 1770; in 1814 he sold his second library, nearly 6,500 volumes, to the U.S. government for $23,950 after British forces burned the Library of Congress.
ev: Born at Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia, the third of ten children
Admitted to the Virginia bar; from 1769 to 1775 he represents Albemarle County in the House of Burgesses
Writes most of the Declaration of Independence between 11 and 28 June; Congress votes to ratify it on 4 July
Succeeds Benjamin Franklin as Minister to France, having arrived in Paris in 1784
Elected president by the House of Representatives after thirty-six ballots and sworn in on 4 March
The Louisiana Purchase treaty, signed on 30 April, doubles the size of the United States
Founds the University of Virginia, which opens in 1825 with Jefferson as its first rector
Dies at Monticello on 4 July, the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence

sections.early:
Thomas Jefferson was born on 13 April 1743 (2 April 1743, Old Style) at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia, the third of ten children. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a planter and surveyor; his mother was Jane Randolph. The family moved to Tuckahoe Plantation in 1745 and returned to Shadwell before October 1753. Jefferson was taught by tutors and at an English school from the age of five, and from 1758 to 1760 he boarded with the family of the Reverend James Maury, studying history, science and the classics. He came to know visitors to Shadwell such as the Cherokee chief Ostenaco, and in Williamsburg he met Patrick Henry.

His father died in 1757, and Jefferson inherited approximately 5,000 acres, which included the land on which he later built Monticello. In 1761 he entered the College of William & Mary, where he studied mathematics and philosophy with William Small and encountered the ideas of John Locke, Francis Bacon and Isaac Newton. Small introduced him to George Wythe and Francis Fauquier. Jefferson concluded his formal studies in April 1762 and read the law under Wythe. In October 1765 his sister Jane died at the age of 25, and he spent months in mourning. He amassed three libraries in his lifetime; the first, of about 200 volumes, was destroyed in a fire at Shadwell in 1770.
sections.rise:
In 1767 Jefferson was admitted to the Virginia bar. Between 1769 and 1775 he represented Albemarle County in the House of Burgesses. In 1769 he wrote and sponsored legislation to give masters of slaves the discretion to emancipate them, which faced strong opposition in a largely agrarian state. As a lawyer he took on seven freedom-seeking enslaved people as clients, and in one case argued that everyone comes into the world with a right to his own person; the judge cut him off and ruled against his client. In 1774 he wrote a resolution calling for a boycott of British goods in protest at the Intolerable Acts, which was expanded into A Summary View of the Rights of British America.

In 1768 he began building Monticello. On 1 January 1772 he married Martha Wayles Skelton, a 23-year-old widow. When her father died in 1773 the couple inherited 135 enslaved people, 11,000 acres and the estate's debts. Elected to the Second Continental Congress in 1775, Jefferson was one of its youngest delegates at 33. John Adams supported his appointment to the Committee of Five, and persuaded the committee to choose him to write the Declaration of Independence. He wrote most of it in isolation between 11 and 28 June 1776. Congress removed roughly a fourth of his draft, a change he resented but did not speak of publicly, and on 4 July 1776 voted unanimously to ratify it.
sections.deeds:
In the Virginia House of Delegates from 1776 Jefferson drafted 126 bills in three years, including laws to streamline the judicial system and to end entail and primogeniture. His Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom, drafted in 1777, was ratified in 1786 as the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom. He was governor in 1779 and 1780 and moved the capital from Williamsburg to Richmond. In Congress in 1783 and 1784 he was the principal author of the Land Ordinance of 1784, which proposed dividing the western territory into future states and banning slavery there; Congress rejected the ban, and its provisions were modified into the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. His Notes on the State of Virginia was first published in 1785, and from 1784 to 1789 he served in Paris, succeeding Benjamin Franklin as Minister to France.

Jefferson became the first Secretary of State in 1790 and resigned in December 1793. He and James Madison founded the Democratic-Republican Party in 1792. He was elected president in 1800, and the House chose him on 17 February 1801. He cut the national debt from $83 million to $57 million with Albert Gallatin, shrank the navy and signed the act founding West Point. In 1803 the United States bought 827,987 square miles from France for $15 million. Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark west in 1804, and in 1807 he signed the Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves.
sections.opponents:
As secretary of state Jefferson opposed Alexander Hamilton's plans for a national debt and a national bank, and the dispute nearly led Washington to dismiss him from the cabinet. In the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, written anonymously with Madison, he advocated nullification; the biographer Ron Chernow contends that they were "a recipe for disunion", and Washington told Patrick Henry that they would "dissolve the union or produce coercion". His Embargo Act of 1807 triggered economic chaos and was strongly criticised, and he abandoned it a year later. He ordered Aaron Burr's arrest for treason, told Congress that Burr's guilt was "beyond question" and denounced his acquittal.

On Native Americans, Jefferson held that they were equal in body and mind to Europeans but inferior in culture and technology, and told his secretary of war that if the United States had to fight a tribe, it would not stop "until that tribe is exterminated or driven beyond the Mississippi". Historians such as Peter S. Onuf and Merrill D. Peterson argue that his policies did little to promote assimilation and were a pretext to seize lands. On slavery, he enslaved about 600 people over his lifetime and sold approximately 110 for economic reasons; in 1792 he calculated a 4 percent yearly profit on the birth of black children, and Brion Davis writes that his emancipation efforts virtually ceased. In Notes he wrote of his "suspicion" that Black people were mentally and physically inferior. His administration refused to recognise Haiti.
sections.last:
After the presidency Jefferson remained in correspondence with the country's leaders, including Madison and James Monroe. He founded the University of Virginia in 1819, organised its charter campaign, designed its buildings and planned its curriculum, and served as its first rector when it opened in 1825. After a decade without contact, he and John Adams resumed writing in 1812 and exchanged 158 letters over the next 14 years. In 1821 he began his Autobiography. In November 1824 he was reunited at Monticello with the Marquis de Lafayette.

Debts of approximately $100,000 weighed on him in his final months, and in February 1826 he successfully applied to the General Assembly to hold a public lottery as a fundraiser. His health had begun to deteriorate in July 1825, and by June 1826 he was confined to bed. He died on 4 July 1826 at 12:50 p.m., aged 83, on the 50th anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration; John Adams died the same day, his last words being "Thomas Jefferson survives". Jefferson was interred at Monticello under an epitaph he wrote, naming the Declaration, the Statute for Religious Freedom and the University of Virginia and leaving out his political offices. His will freed five male Hemings slaves, but his estate, possessions and slaves were sold at public auctions starting in 1827, and Monticello was sold in 1831.
sections.legacy:
Jefferson's political outlook became known as Jeffersonian democracy, and his Democratic-Republican Party dominated early American politics. He is regarded as an icon of individual liberty, democracy and republicanism. Historians describe the Declaration as among the most significant documents in world history; David Armitage has written that "No American document has had a greater global impact". Jack Rakove argues that "all men are created equal" did not originally refer to individual equality but to the colonists' right as a people to self-government, while Henry Wiencek notes that Jefferson included slaves when he wrote it. The Statute for Religious Freedom and his reference to "a wall of separation between Church and State" have been cited in later debates; the Supreme Court has cited the latter phrase several times in interpreting the Establishment Clause.

Scholars give radically differing interpretations of his relationship with slavery, from "emancipationists" who see an early proto-abolitionist making pragmatic compromises, to "revisionists" who argue that he entrenched the institution. On Sally Hemings, the Thomas Jefferson Foundation concluded after a 1998 DNA study that he likely fathered all her children listed at Monticello, and most historians now hold that he fathered her son Eston; a minority of scholars maintain that the evidence is insufficient to prove it. In October 2021 New York City's Public Design Commission voted to remove a plaster model of his statue from the City Council chamber, citing his fathering of children with people he enslaved.

summary: Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826), a Virginia planter and lawyer, wrote most of the Declaration of Independence, served as governor, minister to France and secretary of state, and was the third president of the United States, from 1801 to 1809. He enslaved about 600 people over his lifetime.
references: Richard B. Bernstein, Thomas Jefferson (Oxford University Press, 2003)
John B. Boles, Jefferson: Architect of American Liberty (Basic Books, 2017)
Fawn Brodie, Thomas Jefferson: An Intimate History (W. W. Norton & Company, 1974)
